introduction.text:
The **Basilica Hilariana** is an ancient sanctuary beneath the courtyard of Rome’s Celio military hospital. Dating to the Antonine period in the second century, it served as the meeting place of the dendrophori, a religious association connected with Cybele, the Great Mother, and Attis. Its benefactor was the wealthy merchant Manius Publicius Hilarus, commemorated by an inscribed statue base found inside.

Rooms were arranged around a central courtyard, with a staircase connecting the building to the higher street level. A mosaic from its entrance shows animals surrounding an eye pierced by a spear: an image intended to ward off misfortune. The remains were partly uncovered in 1889 during construction of the hospital; later excavations revealed more of the complex.

history.description: The complex underwent extensive alterations in the third century. From the fourth century, some rooms were used for laundry and dyeing workshops; these activities expanded in the fifth century. The complex was finally abandoned in the sixth century.
Following the discoveries of 1889, large-scale excavations took place between 1987 and 1989. Further work during hospital renovations exposed the complex in 1997.

design.description: A central courtyard was surrounded by rooms used by the association. The building originally had an upper floor, which has not survived. A square feature in the courtyard may have held the sacred pine associated with Cybele and Attis.

art.description: The entrance mosaic depicts animals around a human eye pierced by a spear, a protective image against ill fortune. Removed from the site, it was later held at the Centrale Montemartini.
